Chapter Six: Challenging Assumptions and Everyday Habits.
You know, sometimes the toughest part of making a change is just figuring out what actually needs to change. Most of us go through our routines almost on autopilot—picking up habits from our family, friends, or just the world around us without even realizing it. These habits feel so natural, so automatic, that we hardly notice they're even there... until someone points them out.
Picture this: You're at work, sitting in another one of those meetings. They always seem to unfold the same way, don't they? The loudest voices take over, while others—often women—get interrupted or talked over. Nobody means to silence anyone, but the pattern keeps repeating. Then, one day, a colleague quietly asks, “Hey, did you notice who actually gets to finish their sentences?” And suddenly, what used to be invisible snaps into focus. It's like a light gets switched on.
The same thing can happen at home, too. Imagine a couple splitting up the chores without ever really talking about it. Over time, one person finds themselves doing most of the emotional heavy lifting—remembering birthdays, organizing meals, smoothing out family tensions. It's not that the other person doesn't care—they just never noticed how uneven things had become. When someone finally names it, there's this moment of discomfort, maybe even some defensiveness. But if you're honest about it, that's when the chance for real change appears.
Most people don't set out to be unfair. The problem is, we just aren't taught to spot all those subtle ways that inequality sneaks in. It's so easy to assume everything's fine, that everyone’s happy, until someone speaks up. That’s when the real work gets going—not with some big, dramatic gesture, but with those small, everyday choices.
Sometimes, it’s just about pausing before you make a joke, or noticing who actually gets the credit for new ideas. Maybe it’s as simple as asking, “How can I help?” or “Is this really fair?” These questions don’t always come with easy answers, but they open the door to something better. And over time, new habits start to form—what once felt awkward soon becomes second nature.
Challenging our assumptions isn’t about pointing fingers or blaming anyone. It’s about staying curious, about wanting to see how things could be better. And honestly, most people are surprised by just how much shifts when they start to notice the little things. No, the world won't change overnight. But every small act, every moment of awareness, really does add up.
This journey? It doesn’t end. There will be awkward moments, times you get it wrong, or times you feel a bit exposed. But those aren’t failures—they’re signs you’re growing. The more we question our habits, the more space we create for fairness, respect, and real connection.
